 Selling Your Accounting Practice? Don’t Overlook This Crucial Step
Hi Sara,
So, you’ve decided to sell your accounting practice—congratulations! 
Now, let’s talk about a little wrinkle you might not have anticipated: the AICPA’s 90-day notice requirement for transferring client records.
If you’re unfamiliar with this rule, here’s the gist: even after you’ve sold your business (stock or asset sale—it doesn’t matter), you’re required to notify clients and obtain their consent before transferring their records to the buyer. 
And if they don’t respond at all, you have to wait 90 days before assuming it’s okay.
Sounds simple? 
Sure, until you realize:
That’s 90 days of your buyer paying overhead on a business they can’t fully operate.

It’s also 90 days of dwindling working capital and potentially frustrated clients.

So, how are people navigating this tricky requirement?
Creative Solutions Sellers Are Using (not necessarily solutions I recommend!)
Pre-Closing Partnership: Sellers make the buyer a partner just before closing, transforming the transaction into an internal transfer and sidestepping the 90-day rule entirely.

All Hands on Deck: For smaller client lists, sellers personally call each client, requesting consent and singing the praises of the incoming buyer.

Contractor Stopgap: Sellers retain their LLC post-sale and hire the buyer as a contractor, allowing access to records under the seller’s umbrella until consents are in place.

Each of these options has pros and cons, and some are more feasible than others depending on the size of your client list and the timing of your sale. They are all in the gray area of compliance and may not meet the risk profile of you or your counterparty.
Why This Matters
The rule aims to protect sensitive client data—a noble goal. But its implementation can feel like a logistical headache, especially during tax season when delays could be disastrous.
What You Should Do
If you’re selling your practice:
Understand your client relationships. Do you have an email relationship with your clients? If not, securing consent might be harder than expected and take an enormous amount of effort.

Plan ahead with your buyer. Discuss how you’ll tackle the 90-day hurdle early in the process.

Stay informed about compliance options and be ready to get creative.

At the end of the day, selling your accounting practice is a huge milestone. The right plan—and the right team—can make the process smoother.
Have questions about selling your practice or navigating the AICPA’s notice requirements?

Here’s to Smarter Transitions,
Sara Sharp
Partner, SK&S Law Group
